"He was so humble and self-effacing that he had no idea of his own greatness."

In his autobiography, the late Arthur Arberry writes of the late Reynold A. Nicholson — scholar, commentator, and translator of literary and mystical works from Persian and Arabic into English:

He was a consummate scholar, so enamored of his books that he sacrificed his eyesight to ceaseless reading, so humble and self-effacing that he had no idea of his own greatness. In the final years of his life, when the lamp of his eyes was flickering toward extinction, he composed this verse — a poem that, to me, among all the last words ever uttered by human beings, carries the truest inspiration and the most moving farewell:

When Truth appears unveiled before your eyes,
These tongues are left bewildered and surprised.
*I shall fall silent — the Beloved has come to speak:*
*Listen, and God knows best what is right and true.*
*Become devoid of sense, of hearing, and of thought,*
*That you may hear the summons "Return!"*
As long as this tongue remains, you shall not hear the Word.
So words must be brief. And peace.

**I have borrowed the Persian rendering of Nicholson's poem from verses of the Masnavi. The asterisked lines are from the Masnavi.

- Nicholson's poem, as narrated by Arberry, reads:
When Truth shines out words fail and nothing tell;
Now hear the Voice within your hearts. Farewell.

This is the closing verse of a long poem that Arberry quoted and confirmed earlier in this same piece, noting that in these verses Nicholson was deeply influenced by Rumi: ... He seldom spoke of his personal beliefs, and I, too, in twenty-five years of close friendship with him, learned little about how he was raised or of his spiritual journey. Yet the image that took shape in my mind was that he, like many others, had lost his faith in youth and then recovered it through intellectual companionship and kinship of spirit with Muslim mystics.

In his old age, he composed a poem in which, for the first time, he laid bare his innermost thoughts. It was clear that these thoughts had been profoundly shaped by long years of studying Rumi's works ...

Source: @bamotamem

My grandmother and some AI experts and enthusiasts have something in common

One of the most delightful letters of recent years is one that a number of Fields Medal winners (the same medal through which we know Maryam Mirzakhani) published publicly, without a specific addressee:

A Severe Misalignment of AI in Mathematics

This letter was published at a time when people — most of whom, as it happens, were not experts in mathematics — were excitedly talking in the media and on social networks about AI's ability to solve unsolved mathematical problems (some Erdős problems and a proposed proof for the existence and smoothness of Navier-Stokes).

This excitement is understandable. Understanding mathematics is hard for many of us. Unlike intelligence (which fortunately none of us complain about the distribution of, and we believe we've received a larger share than others), mathematical talent is something we readily admit to lacking.

So it's only natural that a machine being able to solve unsolved problems is astonishing.

Every sentence of the mathematicians' letter is worth reading. It can't be summarized in a Telegram post (we'll review it more carefully later on Motamem).

But if I want to summarize the text in my own words, their point is that in many mathematical problems, more important than "finding the answer" are the solutions, ideas, and methods found along the way, which draw a bigger and clearer picture of the land of mathematics.

Unsolved problems are something like rare veins of gold in a mine. Thousands of problems must be posed and solved so that, among them, a beautiful "unsolved" problem remains — one the new generation of mathematicians can test their strength against and use to discover new territories in the land of mathematics.

A problem that is solved by machine destroys one of these potential opportunities and damages a mine whose resources are not easily replenished.

I remember when we were kids, my grandmother, who apparently had grown tired of the loud sound of the TV broadcasting a football match, muttered in protest: "They should get ten or twenty balls and give them to these young guys so they don't all have to run after one ball like this."

These days, seeing each and every mathematical problem that "burns and is lost" by being solved, and the public joy (outside the community of mathematicians), I remember my grandmother's words. I feel that some people are happy that hundreds of balls have been thrown into the middle of the mathematics football field.

🔴How can we make the most of middle age? We shouldn't expect our past selves to have our present understanding. ✍Mostafa Malekian

Sometimes we look at the past and say: If I had spent those years doing something else, I would have a better life today. Why did I play so much as a child? Why did I pursue things in my youth that no longer matter to me today?

But in this judgment, we forget one thing: every period of life has its own demands. We cannot have had a childhood without having the interests and desires of childhood. We cannot have gone through youth and yet expect to have had our present maturity from the very beginning.

Part of our sorrow about the past comes from this very expectation — as if we wanted to have been as mature throughout our entire lives as we are today. Whereas it is precisely by going through those periods that we have reached this point.

▪️ Let us not see past mistakes as pure loss

Even a choice that we consider a mistake today may have brought us joys and friendships.

For example, we say, why did I pursue football instead of studying? But how much happiness has that same football given us? What friendships did it create that have stayed with us later in life?

If we only look at the costs of a choice and dismiss all the good things that came from it, we will not have a complete picture of the past.

▪️ No life is all benefit and no cost

Every way of life opens up possibilities before us and also carries costs. We cannot compare our lived life with an imaginary life that has all the good things and pays no price for them.

▪️ Let us seize the remaining opportunities

Not all opportunities are lost with the end of youth. There are still things we can begin, things we can learn, and pleasures we can experience.

If we spend today only on regret for yesterday, in a few more years, today will also become a new subject for regret.

Instead of only lamenting lost opportunities, let us treasure the opportunities not yet lost.

Oil transit through Hormuz rises: The White House celebrated, the market didn't buy it
Sadegh Al-Hosseini
Kelley Vlahos, editor of Responsible Statecraft, made important points in yesterday's article that I'll get into below. He says last week the White House and its supporters announced "the strait is open and we've won." On Sunday, however, Brent was still holding at $102. The gap between these two images is what this article is about.
What's really going on behind the numbers? Daily oil transit through Hormuz has reached 13 to 17 million barrels, down from about 20 million before the war. But a large portion of it is happening through an emergency workaround: state-owned ships pass through the strait with their tracking systems turned off and hand off their cargo to supertankers in safe waters. The cost of chartering a supertanker from the Persian Gulf to Asia has hit $1.2 million, insurance has gotten more expensive, and ships carrying fertilizer, aluminum, petrochemicals, and grain are still stranded in the Persian Gulf. America has sent a third aircraft carrier to the region, and its navy is, according to experts, stretched thin.
The drawdown from reserves is also heavy: 400 million barrels drawn from reserves in March, another 100 million barrels from the G7, America's strategic reserves at their lowest level since 1983, and JPMorgan saying it sees no end to this situation.
In other words, Iran can't fully close the strait, and America can't fully open it. Unless Trump reaches a deal with Iran; that's what the market is really waiting for.
Why is this news encouraging for us?
1. Trump's leverage has hit its ceiling. With three aircraft carriers, the strait has only become "half-open." When American experts themselves say the only way out is a deal with Iran, it means the military option costs more than it delivers.
2. The clock is working against the White House. The November midterm elections are approaching, and according to experts, fuel prices won't come down by then; the soaring cost of diesel has even hit American farmers. This pressure raises the incentive for a deal. But it's clear that the cost of this war is being paid by the people of Iran.
3. A deal would untie many knots at once. A world whose reserves have run dry is thirsty for fresh supply; it's not just oil — petrochemicals, fertilizer, and metals are also stuck behind this barrier.
The world has come to believe that Hormuz today is neither closed nor open; and the key is not on warships but on the negotiating table.

🔴 Why do even good things sometimes make us feel bad? ✍️ Mostafa Malekian

We usually assume that if good things happen to us, we'll feel good too. But the pleasantness of an event, in itself, doesn't guarantee that we can handle it well.

We live in a world that can be hard on us in two ways: not everything goes the way we want, and we have no certainty about what's coming.

▪️ The world has no obligation to fulfill our desires

There's no reason all the world's events should conform to our preferences and wishes. Some events are pleasant and some unpleasant; even a single event can make one person happy and another miserable.

Rain is a source of joy for a farmer waiting to water his field; but for a launderer who has hung washed clothes out to dry in the sun, it spells trouble.

The rain is the same rain; what differs is its relation to our desires and circumstances. The world has neither sworn to be our enemy nor promised to always go along with what we want.

▪️ Even joys may show up uninvited

The difficulty isn't just that we dislike certain events; it's also that we don't know what will come, or when.

Suppose you love someone dearly, but they show up at your door unannounced. Despite being happy to see them, you might lose your composure and fail to receive them the way you'd like.

Loving a guest is not the same as being ready for their arrival.

The same holds for the good things in life: we may want something, yet not be prepared for its sudden arrival. As a result, our reaction may be ill-considered and create fresh problems.

▪️ The suffering of the event and the suffering of the reaction

Part of life's difficulty comes from events not matching our desires; another part can stem from how we face them.

If we expect life to always unfold according to our wishes and predictions, we'll be constantly caught off guard. And being caught off guard can push us into reactions that only deepen our suffering.

So we must prepare ourselves to live in a world that holds both adversity and uncertainty—so that we can meet what arrives uninvited with greater composure.

We can't control the arrival of every uninvited guest; but we can learn how to face them.

📚 Mostafa Malekian | A conversation about the book "Welcoming the Unwelcome" by Pema Chödrön

Source: @miladdokhanchi

For complex human problems, we shouldn't be looking for technical answers! If a pipe in your house bursts, that's a technical problem; but when your neighbor puts their trash out earlier than they're supposed to, that's no longer merely technical — it belongs to the realm of human problems. In teaching problem-solving, the first thing we draw the learner's attention to is distinguishing the technical problem from the human problem, and when we talk about problem-solving and teaching it, we mean the second category — because technical problems require expertise in their own field. If my phone stops working, I go to a specialist and they fix it. But human problems don't necessarily have predetermined solutions, and technical expertise alone won't help solve them. The solution to these problems has to be discovered, and solving them requires a basic understanding of the humanities and learning the skill of problem-solving. The biggest mistake is usually offering technical solutions for problems with human roots. When my employees' motivation is low and they show up late to work because of it, I can't force them into line with punishment, incentives, and a few new rules; I need to ask why their motivation has dropped, invite them into a conversation, and address the problem at the level of human relationships. Another mistake is assuming that our technical expertise can help us solve human problems — which it absolutely cannot. Yet another mistake is framing problems with human roots in technical terms. In that same example of lateness, if I say the reason is that they wake up late and that a morning phone call will get them to work on time, I've framed a human problem in technical terms! Mistaking technical problems for human ones and vice versa, offering technical solutions for human problems, and expecting clear technical solutions for complex problems — these are among the greatest plagues of our country's decision-making and problem-solving system. In this regard, the Iranian opposition abroad is hardly innocent either! We Iranians don't have strong problem-solving skills, and at the root of this situation you can feel the hegemony of engineers and physicians, the failure of humanities scholars to engage with concrete problems, and the jurists who want to solve human problems through technical legislation. This pattern shows itself when Hezbollahis are waiting for the leadership to solve the problem, the general public is waiting for the government, and some are waiting for Trump! Oblivious to the fact that solutions are discovered in small settings, and top-down solutions are all doomed to fail. Governments never have solutions for anything, and when they do, they're technical solutions for complex human problems. #Government-Addiction

Likewise, embracing "existential loneliness"—which is intertwined with your and my being—and reducing its volume with the aid of "velvety solitude," migrates lightness and joy toward us. "Humility and hardness" arrive together with high "self-esteem" and "self-worth" and are among the components of adequate mental health. The modern wayfarer neither knows nor presents himself as lower than he is, nor considers and displays himself as higher than he is. He loves himself honestly and realistically, as he is, and with an eye to his endowments, capabilities, successes, weaknesses, misfortunes, and failures, deeply; and does not spend night and day seeking others' approval; rather, in Shamlou's phrase, he dwells at the "glorious altitude of humility" and fills and empties his lungs with its pure air. The core message is that Iran today, in the narrative being presented, is not an Iran that can be dragged back to its former position of dependency. This is no small distinction. In the text, three temporal planes are woven together: a past that must not return, a present that must be defended, and a future that must be more powerful than the present. That is why the message does not conclude in the past either; it moves toward the future. But it is precisely here that the most difficult question begins. "We will not go back" is not merely a statement about a foreign enemy. Not going back cannot be measured solely by missile range, the distance of enemy warships, or military operational capacity. If we take the concept of power seriously, then the economy, knowledge, technology, the quality of governance, public trust, human capital, social cohesion, and the ability to solve problems are all part of that same arena. A country that does not want to go back must be able to simultaneously withstand external threats and, on the domestic front, create the capacity for a better life, greater hope, and the possibility of broader progress. This is where the narrative of power meets people's everyday experience. The narrower the gap between the two, the more the phrase "we will not go back" transforms from a political slogan into a collective experience. The wider this gap grows, the less the foreign enemy even needs to challenge the narrative; people's daily lives will do it for them. The recent message can be read from various angles. One can debate its claim to power, the Strait of Hormuz, regional resistance, or its religious symbolism. But the thread binding all these elements together is, to my mind, too clear to be lost in noisy headlines: "The enemy wants Iran to return to the past; the text says that past is over." The question of Iran's future lies in exactly the same place: let us not go back — not only in independence and security, but in every component that truly makes a nation powerful.

Let us revive leadership!

Within each of us dwells a sultan and a shepherd. The sultan rules and controls; the inner shepherd guides. The sultan leans toward subjugation, domination, and the management of affairs, while the shepherd leans toward guidance, opening new horizons, and stepping into the unknown.

In the language of business, the inner sultan manages and the shepherd leads. The sultan is necessary for managing affairs; the shepherd, for creation, bringing forth, and breaking down the walls of human limitation. Sultanhood gravitates toward the individual; shepherdliness, toward the collective.

In the duality of sultan and shepherd, the question is not one of preference but of balance — and balance becomes possible when we have not only erected the apparatuses of our inner sultanate but also passed beyond them and brought inner leadership into emergence. Yes, both the sultan and the shepherd are needed, but if we are to envision an ultimate destination, that destination is the passage from the inner sultanate to the inner shepherdliness.

Shepherdliness and leadership, then, are not a position. Leadership is a particular way of thinking and being; leadership is a path — in the first instance a personal path that then becomes determinate outwardly and takes on a collective form. The question: shepherd or sultan?

In the process leading to the Islamic Revolution, Iranian society managed to pass beyond sultanate and activate its inner shepherd — and it was this discovered inner shepherd that emerged outwardly, and from its heart, the concept of "Imam" was born. In Iran, leadership emerged because every human being saw themselves as a leader; because leadership emerged as a way of being; because an inner revolution took place in our inner states, and this caused leadership as a collective matter to also appear in Article 43 of the Constitution: "The organization of the country's economic program... such that every individual... has sufficient ability to participate actively in the leadership of the country..."

But in post-revolutionary Iran, leadership was reduced to a position. Once again our inner sultanic relations were activated, and we were degraded from leaders who discovered "leaders" to followers who merely follow. From then on, following, imitation, and the rejection of responsibility became our common behavioral currency. Everywhere: politics, art, culture, economy...

To solve Iran's problems, each of us must first and once again become a leader. We must pass beyond our inner sultanates and activate our inner shepherds; and it is these inner shepherds that, when actualized, make shepherdliness possible outwardly. Without leadership as a plural matter, political and social leadership is also impossible; what emerges without it is not leadership — it is the same sultan wearing the shepherd's clothing.

Let us activate our inner shepherd.

Let us all be leaders.

▫️Two.
Every foot that entered the house found a treasure;
No longer would all its life be at the market.
(Saadi)
There is a treasure that is found in the realm of the heart. One who finds the way to the inner treasure is freed from dependence on markets. Bayazid Bastami said about the meaning of dervishhood: "The one who, in the corner of his own heart, finds a foot entering a treasure..."

▫️Three.
One who became a stranger to wealth and greatness and lordship,
Is familiar to whomever he reaches.
(Saadi)
One who sees himself free from names and positions and passing powers can be familiar and close to everyone. If we are captivated by our own greatness and lordship and wealth, if we are bound by our position and name and reputation and intelligence and knowledge, we lose the felicity of "familiarity."

▫️Four.
Whoever does not know gratitude for today's blessing
Will eat regret upon the portion of tomorrow's mercy.
(Saadi)
One who does not appreciate the gifts of this world and does not welcome them with gratitude and joy will also be deprived of the mercy of the next world.

Whoever does not see today in the world the countenance of the Friend,
It is most likely that tomorrow he will have no vision.
(Saadi)
The beauty of nature and the movement and growth of the earth is a mercy of this world:
"Fa-unzur ila athar rahmatillah kayfa yuhyi al-arda ba'da mawtiha" (Surah Rum, verse 50)
"Look at these signs of Allah's kindness, how He revives the earth after its death." (Translation of Tafsir Kashf al-Asrar)

▫️Five.
Except the remembrance of the Friend, whatever you do is wasted life;
Except the secret of love, whatever you say is vanity.
(Saadi)
If life is not mixed with the remembrance of the Friend, and is not spent in longing for the Friend, it is wasted. It has passed in vanity:
Saadi, if he does not risk love, what shall he do with the kingdom of existence?
It is a pity that a whole life should go to waste.

The remembrance and recollection of the Friend has no end. It is not tiresome either. Because it is the food of the soul. The bread and water of the soul:
Our speech grew long and still remains,
For the remembrance of the Friend brings no weariness whatsoever.
(Saadi)
Therefore, his regret is for the times that passed unaware of the Friend:
Whatever we said other than the tale of the Friend,
In all our life we regret it.
(Saadi)
If there is any regret, it is nothing but this: why did we not breathe in His remembrance more? Why did we not throb in longing for Him more?
So that precious life does not end in regret,
All night Your remembrance was ongoing and repeated.

Speaking with Him, speaking of Him, and floating in the "tale of the Friend" is the meaning of life.
